claim: The shotgun sequencing approach creates unbiased genomic data that can be leveraged across populations and generations despite evolutionary divergence.
source: Our shotgun sequencing approach alleviates many challenges that are associated with traditional PCR- and amplicon-based approaches, including the risk of allelic dropout due to scarce or fragmented DNA (Smith and Wang, 2014) and amplification of closely related species (Wilcox et al., 2013), while simultaneously avoiding laborious and expensive pre-processing of DNA such as required for DNA hybridization capture and creating unbiased genomic data that can be leveraged across populations and generations despite evolutionary divergence.
evidence: Stated as an advantage of the approach

claim: Less than a gram of surface soil allows for highly accurate kākāpō monitoring while detecting additional 20 species.
source: We show that less than a gram of surface soil allows for highly accurate kākāpō monitoring while detecting additional 20 species, including the elusive and threatened New Zealand lesser short-tailed bat (Mystacina tuberculata), and invasive mouse and possum species.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data presented in the study

claim: The New Zealand lesser short-tailed bat (Mystacina tuberculata) is elusive and threatened.
source: We show that less than a gram of surface soil allows for highly accurate kākāpō monitoring while detecting additional 20 species, including the elusive and threatened New Zealand lesser short-tailed bat (Mystacina tuberculata), and invasive mouse and possum species.
evidence: Stated as fact in the manuscript

claim: A few reads of the invasive Polynesian rat (Rattus exulans) were detected on Whenua Hou.
source: We importantly detected a few reads of the invasive Polynesian rat (Rattus exulans) on Whenua Hou, which serves as a predator-free sanctuary for the surviving kākāpō population.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Whenua Hou serves as a predator-free sanctuary for the surviving kākāpō population.
source: We importantly detected a few reads of the invasive Polynesian rat (Rattus exulans) on Whenua Hou, which serves as a predator-free sanctuary for the surviving kākāpō population.
evidence: Stated as fact in the manuscript

claim: The rat genomic material might have been transported to the island via avian predators.
source: As we only found very weak evidence in only one sample, we however postulate that the rat genomic material might have been transported to the island via avian predators.
evidence: Stated as a hypothesis

claim: Contamination with R. exulans DNA could have happened in the laboratory which handles ancient R. exulans samples.
source: Alternatively, contamination could have happened in the laboratory which handles ancient R. exulans samples.
evidence: Stated as an alternative hypothesis

claim: The soil eDNA approach has a high spatial and temporal resolution.
source: Our soil eDNA approach has a high spatial and temporal resolution, as shown by the rapid drop in signal with increasing distance from kākāpō hotspots and by the scarcity of kākāpō DNA in recently abandoned nests.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing signal drop with distance and time

claim: The approach can distinguish DNA from kākāpō from its closest relatives, the Nestor parrots kea and kākā.
source: We show that our approach can distinguish DNA from kākāpō from its closest relatives, the Nestor parrots kea and kākā: We, as expected, did not find any kākāpō signal in the artificial Nestor aviaries, but evidence of Nestor, human, exotic birds, and mammalian pest DNA.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from aviary samples

claim: The low proportion of target DNA in soil samples (<0.1%) makes standard 'non-selective' nanopore sequencing more efficient than selective nanopore sequencing at producing species-specific sequencing reads.
source: We importantly observe that the low proportion of target DNA in our soil samples (<0.1%) makes standard 'non-selective" nanopore sequencing even more efficient than selective nanopore sequencing (aka 'adaptive sampling') at producing species-specific sequencing reads.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Table 1

claim: When the target DNA is less than 0.1% in the selective sequencing approach, more time will be spent on read-unblocking than sequencing target DNA.
source: When the target DNA is less than 0.1% in the selective sequencing approach, more time will be spent on read-unblocking than sequencing target DNA (internal communications with ONT).
evidence: Supported by internal communications with ONT

claim: Selective nanopore sequencing will rapidly increase in efficiency, resulting in reduced pore-clogging and potentially faster decision-making with less sequencing efforts spent on read-unblocking.
source: We, however, anticipate that selective nanopore sequencing will rapidly increase in efficiency, resulting in reduced pore-clogging and potentially faster decision-making with less sequencing efforts spent on read-unblocking.
evidence: Stated as an anticipation/prediction

claim: Selective nanopore sequencing brings the prospect of targeting finer scales, such as selecting specific chromosomes or genomic regions that are highly representative of a species' genome-wide diversity.
source: Selective nanopore sequencing further brings the prospect of targeting finer scales, such as selecting specific chromosomes or genomic regions that are highly representative of a species' genome-wide diversity.
evidence: Stated as a prospect/potential application

claim: Standard non-selective nanopore sequencing allows for within-species assessments across multiple taxa, combining species detection with within-species monitoring.
source: Standard non-selective nanopore sequencing can, on the other hand, be advantageous since it allows for within-species assessments across multiple taxa, combining species detection with within-species monitoring.
evidence: Stated as an advantage of the approach

claim: Nanopore sequencing can provide a more holistic view of an ecosystem by simultaneously assessing its microbiome.
source: We also show that nanopore sequencing can provide a more holistic view of an ecosystem by simultaneously assessing its microbiome by successfully ascertaining the soil's characteristic bacterial composition.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on bacterial composition

claim: The haplotype agreement scores require an exact overlap between soil- and population-based haplotypes to stringently account for nanopore sequencing errors.
source: As our haplotype agreement scores require an exact overlap between soil- and population-based haplotypes to stringently account for nanopore sequencing errors, the number of remaining haplotypes is sparse (ranging from 21 to 30).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: The number of remaining haplotypes is sparse (ranging from 21 to 30).
source: As our haplotype agreement scores require an exact overlap between soil- and population-based haplotypes to stringently account for nanopore sequencing errors, the number of remaining haplotypes is sparse (ranging from 21 to 30).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The approach can be more lenient in the future given the increasing accuracy of nanopore sequencing of >99%.
source: We anticipate that this approach can be more lenient in the future given the increasing accuracy of nanopore sequencing of >99%.
evidence: Stated as an anticipation based on technological improvements

claim: A larger number of haplotypes might allow covering a larger proportion of the genome and discerning family relationships more accurately.
source: A larger number of haplotypes might then allow us to cover a larger proportion of the genome and to discern family relationships more accurately.
evidence: Stated as a potential future improvement

claim: The current approach was not able to discern the genomic signal of the kākāpō Nora and her offspring.
source: This could resolve individual identification in highly inbred populations, which has been limited in our current approach where we were not able to discern the genomic signal of the kākāpō Nora and her offspring.
evidence: Stated as a limitation of the current approach

claim: The accuracy of the presented approach is already sufficient for delineating families and subpopulations in a wild species.
source: We, however, anticipate that the accuracy of our presented approach is already sufficient for delineating families and subpopulations in a wild species, allowing for in-depth population-based conservation management.
evidence: Stated as an anticipation based on the experimental results

claim: Bayesian inference approaches for conditional genetic stock identification were leveraged to infer contributions of kākāpō individuals to the soil sample.
source: We also leveraged Bayesian inference approaches for conditional genetic stock identification to infer contributions of kākāpō individuals to the soil sample.
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: The Bayesian inference approach together with maximum likelihood estimations confirmed the unexpected detection of the kākāpō Sinbad in the samples.
source: This approach together with our maximum likelihood estimations of the number of contributing individuals confirmed the unexpected detection of the kākāpō Sinbad in our samples.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and metadata

claim: The approach can accurately describe mixtures of individuals.
source: This shows that our approach can accurately describe mixtures of individuals, which will be essential for monitoring non-territorial and migrating species.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results

claim: Nanopore sequencing can enable real-time in-depth monitoring of wild populations, both on the level of species variety and individual genomic variability.
source: We here show that nanopore sequencing can enable real-time in-depth monitoring of wild populations, both on the level of species variety and individual genomic variability.
evidence: Supported by the experimental data presented in the study

claim: It might be feasible to assess the genetic health and adaptive potential of wild populations in a completely non-invasive manner.
source: This further indicates that it might be feasible to assess the genetic health and adaptive potential of wild populations in a completely non-invasive manner.
evidence: Stated as a potential implication of the study

claim: The approach will directly assist the kākāpō conservationists in monitoring individuals in an efficient and non-invasive manner.
source: Our approach will, as a tangible example, directly assist the kākāpō conservationists in monitoring individuals in an efficient and non-invasive manner, and in detecting potentially remnant populations in the wild.
evidence: Stated as a potential application of the study

claim: The approach will assist in detecting potentially remnant kākāpō populations in the wild.
source: Our approach will, as a tangible example, directly assist the kākāpō conservationists in monitoring individuals in an efficient and non-invasive manner, and in detecting potentially remnant populations in the wild.
evidence: Stated as a potential application of the study

claim: The integrated application of eDNA to detect endangered and invasive species and to monitor individuals and subpopulations in endangered populations has the potential to substantially aid universal conservation management around the globe.
source: Even more importantly, we show that the integrated application of eDNA to detect endangered and invasive species and to monitor individuals and subpopulations in endangered populations has the potential to substantially aid universal conservation management around the globe.
evidence: Stated as a potential broader impact of the study

claim: Soil sampling was performed on Whenua Hou, New Zealand, on February 27, 2019.
source: Soil sampling was performed on Whenua Hou, New Zealand, the island with the largest kākāpō population (Figure 4a), on February 27, 2019.
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: Whenua Hou is the island with the largest kākāpō population.
source: Soil sampling was performed on Whenua Hou, New Zealand, the island with the largest kākāpō population (Figure 4a), on February 27, 2019.
evidence: Stated as fact in the manuscript

claim: Sites of interest sampled included male display sites, recently abandoned nests (~30 days), and supplementary feeding stations.
source: We sampled sites of interest, including male display sites (shallow bowls in the ground that are frequented by males every night during breeding seasons), recently abandoned nests (~30 days), and supplementary feeding stations.
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: Male display sites are shallow bowls in the ground that are frequented by males every night during breeding seasons.
source: We sampled sites of interest, including male display sites (shallow bowls in the ground that are frequented by males every night during breeding seasons), recently abandoned nests (~30 days), and supplementary feeding stations.
evidence: Stated as fact in the manuscript

claim: Two replicates were taken at each site.
source: Per site, a new set of nitrile gloves was used for sample collection, debris and leaf litter were removed and a finger-full of soil (~5–10 g) from the surface was put into a small sterile plastic bag; two replicates were taken at each site and subsequently stored in a medium-sized bag to avoid cross-contamination across replicates.
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: Samples and respective replicates were additionally taken at distances of 4 and 20 m per site.
source: Per site, samples and respective replicates were additionally taken at distances of 4 and 20 m.
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: All samples were frozen at –20 °C as soon as possible (at the latest after five hours).
source: All samples per site were stored in a large plastic bag to avoid cross-contamination across sites, and frozen at –20 °C as soon as possible (at the latest after five hours).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: Altogether, 37 samples were taken at six sites.
source: Altogether, 37 samples were taken at six sites (Supplementary file 1; Figure 4b).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: Soil was additionally sampled in aviaries of the kea (Nestor notabilis) and kākā (Nestor meridionalis) in the Dunedin Botanic Garden on September 18, 2020.
source: We additionally sampled soil in aviaries of the kākāpō's two closest relative species, the kea (Nestor notabilis) and kākā (Nestor meridionalis). We sampled two aviaries per species in the Dunedin Botanic Garden, Dunedin, New Zealand, on September 18, 2020.
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: The kea (Nestor notabilis) and kākā (Nestor meridionalis) are the kākāpō's two closest relative species.
source: We additionally sampled soil in aviaries of the kākāpō's two closest relative species, the kea (Nestor notabilis) and kākā (Nestor meridionalis).
evidence: Stated as fact in the manuscript

claim: DNA was extracted from the soil samples using Qiagen's DNeasy PowerSoil Pro kit.
source: DNA was extracted from the Whenua Hou (n=37) and Botanic Garden (n=4) soil samples using Qiagen's DNeasy PowerSoil Pro kit following the manufacturer's recommendations for extraction of genomic DNA from average-wet soil (recommended amount of 250 mg; for exact amounts of soil, see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: Extraction negative controls (deionized water) were included in every extraction run (n=5) to ensure no contamination was introduced during the extraction process.
source: In addition, extraction negative controls (deionized water) were included in every extraction run (n=5) to ensure no contamination was introduced during the extraction process (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: The extracted DNA concentration was measured using the Qubit 4 Fluorometer.
source: The extracted DNA concentration was measured using the Qubit 4 Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) (Supplementary file 1) and stored at –20 °C.
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: DNA quality/quantity analysis, adapter-fusion, indexing and amplification were carried out in single-step quantitative PCR reactions on an Applied Biosystems QuantStudio 1 qPCR instrument.
source: DNA quality/quantity analysis, adapter-fusion, indexing and amplification were carried out in single-step quantitative PCR reactions on an Applied Biosystems QuantStudio 1 qPCR instrument.
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: DNA extracts were PCR-amplified using the "RV" fusion-tag mitochondrial 12 S rRNA-V5 ecoPrimers for the detection of bird, mammalian and fish species.
source: DNA extracts were PCR-amplified using the "RV" fusion-tag mitochondrial 12 S rRNA-V5 ecoPrimers for the detection of bird, mammalian and fish species (RV forward primer: 3`-AATGATACGGCGACCACCGAGATCTACACTGACGACATGGTTCTACAXXXXXXXXGACGTTAGATACCCCACTATGC-5`; RV reverse primer: 5`-CAAGCAGAAGACGGCATACGAGATXXXXXXXX TAGAACAGGCTCCTCTAG-3`; adapted from Riaz et al., 2011; shown with Illumina P5 and P7 adapter sequences underlined, Illumina TruSeq sequencing primer-binding site unmarked, 8 bp unique index tags as X strings and locus-specific primers in bold).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology, adapted from Riaz et al., 2011

claim: All 8 bp index tags differed from each other by at least 3 bp.
source: All 8 bp index tags differed from each other by at least 3 bp.
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: The library was loaded onto an iSeq i1 V2 reagent cartridge with a 300-cycle flow cell with 5% Phi X and run for 290 cycles in a single direction on an Illumina iSeq 100.
source: The library was then loaded onto an iSeq i1 V2 reagent cartridge with a 300-cycle flow cell (Illumina) with 5% Phi X and run for 290 cycles in a single direction on an Illumina iSeq 100 (see Supplementary file 2 for number of sequencing reads).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: The iSeq output FASTQ files were de-multiplexed using the R programming language, using the insect package v1.4.0.
source: The iSeq output FASTQ files were de-multiplexed using the R programming language (R Development Core Team, 2021), using the insect package v1.4.0 (Wilkinson et al., 2018) trimmed sequences were filtered to produce a table of exact ASVs using DADA2 (Callahan et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology with citations

claim: Trimmed sequences were filtered to produce a table of exact ASVs using DADA2.
source: The iSeq output FASTQ files were de-multiplexed using the R programming language (R Development Core Team, 2021), using the insect package v1.4.0 (Wilkinson et al., 2018) trimmed sequences were filtered to produce a table of exact ASVs using DADA2 (Callahan et al., 2016).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology with citation to Callahan et al., 2016

claim: One library per sample was loaded onto an R9.4.1 flow cell and run for approximately 12 hr on a GridION Mk1.
source: We then loaded one library per sample onto an R9.4.1 flow cell and ran them for approximately 12 hr on a GridION Mk1, using the FAST basecalling mode and the high-quality kākāpō reference genome (NCBI taxonomy ID: 2489341) as digital target sequence template (Table 2).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: Guppy v3.2 was used for high accuracy (HAC) basecalling and adapter trimming of all passed output reads.
source: We used Guppy v3.2 (Wick et al., 2019) for high accuracy (HAC) basecalling and adapter trimming of all passed output reads (across all selective sequencing decisions, including 'unblock' for rejected reads, 'no_decision' for reads that were too short for a decision to be taken, and 'stop_receiving' for accepted reads).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology with citation to Wick et al., 2019

claim: Nanofilt v2.6 was used to filter all reads for quality (Q-score >7).
source: We then used Nanofilt v2.6 (De Coster et al., 2018) to filter all reads for quality (Q-score >7) and aligned all reads to the kākāpō reference genome using minimap2 v2.17 (Li, 2018).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology with citation to De Coster et al., 2018

claim: All reads were aligned to the kākāpō reference genome using minimap2 v2.17.
source: We then used Nanofilt v2.6 (De Coster et al., 2018) to filter all reads for quality (Q-score >7) and aligned all reads to the kākāpō reference genome using minimap2 v2.17 (Li, 2018).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology with citation to Li, 2018

claim: SAMtools v1.10 was used to transform the resulting sam files to sorted bam files, filter the bam files for mapped reads, index them and count the number of mapped reads.
source: We then used SAMtools v1.10 (Li et al., 2009) to transform the resulting sam files to sorted bam files, filter the bam files for mapped reads, index them and count the number of mapped reads.
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology with citation to Li et al., 2009

claim: Medaka v1.2.5 was used to call variants against the reference genome using medaka_variant.
source: We used Medaka v1.2.5 (nanoporetech, 2019) to call variants against the reference genome using medaka_variant; medaka_variant intrinsically uses WhatsHap (Martin et al., 2016) to estimate the underlying haplotypes per genomic site.
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology with citations to nanoporetech, 2019 and Martin et al., 2016

claim: medaka_variant intrinsically uses WhatsHap to estimate the underlying haplotypes per genomic site.
source: We used Medaka v1.2.5 (nanoporetech, 2019) to call variants against the reference genome using medaka_variant; medaka_variant intrinsically uses WhatsHap (Martin et al., 2016) to estimate the underlying haplotypes per genomic site.
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology with citation to Martin et al., 2016

claim: The existing population variant callset was produced by the Kākāpō125+consortium by applying DeepVariant to the genomic dataset of nearly the entire kākāpō population (n=169 out of 171 alive kākāpō as of 31/12/2018).
source: Briefly, the existing population variant callset was produced by the Kākāpō125+consortium by applying DeepVariant (Poplin et al., 2018) to the genomic dataset of nearly the entire kākāpō population (n=169 out of 171 alive kākāpō as of 31/12/2018) and by filtering the resulting high-quality variant set for genotype missingness of <20% and a minor allele frequency >1% (resulting in 1,612,477 variants; Guhlin et al., 2022).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology with citations to Poplin et al., 2018 and Guhlin et al., 2022

claim: The population variant callset was filtered for genotype missingness of <20% and a minor allele frequency >1%, resulting in 1,612,477 variants.
source: Briefly, the existing population variant callset was produced by the Kākāpō125+consortium by applying DeepVariant (Poplin et al., 2018) to the genomic dataset of nearly the entire kākāpō population (n=169 out of 171 alive kākāpō as of 31/12/2018) and by filtering the resulting high-quality variant set for genotype missingness of <20% and a minor allele frequency >1% (resulting in 1,612,477 variants; Guhlin et al., 2022).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology with citation to Guhlin et al., 2022

claim: The R package rubias v0.3.2 was used to apply Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methodology with a uniform prior distribution for estimating mixture proportions and individual posterior probabilities of assignment through MCMC iterations conditional on the reference allele frequencies (2000 iterations; burn-in of 100).
source: We additionally used the R package rubias v0.3.2 (Moran and Anderson, 2019) to apply Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methodology with a uniform prior distribution for estimating mixture proportions and individual posterior probabilities of assignment through MCMC iterations conditional on the reference allele frequencies (2000 iterations; burn-in of 100).
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology with citation to Moran and Anderson, 2019

claim: Contributor analyses were performed to estimate the most likely number of kākāpō individuals contributing to each sample using a combinatorial maximum likelihood analysis based on haplotypes.
source: We performed contributor analyses to estimate the most likely number of kākāpō individuals contributing to each sample. We used a combinatorial maximum likelihood analysis based on our haplotypes, with the likelihood of each combination of individuals being calculated as the product of per-haplotype probability.
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology

claim: The taxonomic origin of the background DNA produced by nanopore sequencing approach was assessed using ONT's cloud-based EPI2ME's What's in my Pot (WIMP) platform.
source: We finally assessed the taxonomic origin of the background DNA produced by nanopore sequencing approach (i.e., reads classified as 'unblock' or 'no_decision') using ONT's cloud-based EPI2ME's What's in my Pot (WIMP) (Juul et al., 2015) platform.
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology with citation to Juul et al., 2015

claim: All plots were produced in Python, using Matplotlib v1.5.3.
source: All plots were produced in Python, using Matplotlib v1.5.3.
evidence: Stated as part of the methodology
